question: The creation of the station, on a 15 500-acre site in the Antichasia area, will have disastrous consequences for the environment and for agricultural production, since the thousands of acres of arable land and pastures that will be expropriated for the creation of the project will deprive it of useful agricultural products.

The promotion of the huge photovoltaic power station is another example of deadlock brought about by the EU's strategy of ‘green development’, which is being implemented by the current New Democracy Government as it was by previous ones, as well as by the municipal and regional authorities supported by these parties. The designated area surrounds entire villages, homes and arable and livestock farms.

Also, the project is located in an area where there are two Natura 2000 areas and other protected areas, such as the Drinking Water Protected Area of the Paliosamarina - Voula system. What is the Commission’s position on: 1.

the request of residents to stop the photovoltaic power plant project in an area of high agricultural productivity but also of exceptional natural beauty and cultural significance, which is a result of the implementation of the ‘Green Deal’ which dictates investments in RES with the sole criterion of increasing the profitability of European ‘green business groups’?

the fact that the working and popular classes will not only not benefit from this development, but it will exacerbate their predicament, including energy poverty, as a result of the very same ‘green transition’ and the liberation of energy?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2025) The Environmental Impact Assessment Directive1 requires that projects likely to have significant effects on the environment by virtue, inter alia, of their nature, size or location be subject to an assessment of their environmental effects.

For the categories listed in Annex II of this Directive, such as photovoltaic (PV) plants2, the authorities must determine whether an assessment is necessary through a case-by-case study or through previously set thresholds or criteria. This assessment is under the responsibility of the national authorities for the individual case, such as the one of this project.

The Commission noted in the Vision for Agriculture and Food3 the limited availability of fertile land in a context of growing competition for its use. In response, the Commission is working towards launching an EU observatory on Farmland to enhance transparency in land use changes and, among others, will help Member States take informed decisions on the regulation of farmland markets.

Locally available renewables such as solar PV can contribute to produce electricity at lower prices than fossil fuels and to lower energy prices for local communities. EU legislation encourages the participation of local communities in renewable energy projects, which can take several forms, including benefit sharing mechanisms4.
It also encourages Member States to tackle energy poverty by prioritising vulnerable and low-income households in energy efficiency and building renovation projects.

Finally, mindful of the need to balance energy production with other public interests, the Commission has issued recommendations and guidance for Member States on promoting innovative technologies and forms of renewable energy deployment5, like agrivoltaics.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment.
